messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night it happened, the argument in their shared apartment had spiraled past words into heavy, sudden violence. When the door finally gave way, his partner dragged him onto the sidewalk and pressed him against the metal frame of a bus shelter. The glass was cold and unyielding against his ribs. He felt the heavy grip on his shoulders, the hot breath near his ear, the whispered threats about what would happen if he tried to leave. The rumble of a passing bus vibrated through the shelter, shaking the exact spot on his collarbone where fingers had dug in. Minutes later, sirens cut through the tension, but the moment did not end when the police arrived. It settled into him. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that people could not be trusted, and that he was inadequate for surviving it without more force. He would sit in quiet rooms long after the noise had faded, dwelling on what he had done wrong, analyzing his tone, his posture, his choices, certain that if he had only acted differently, the violence would never have reached this point. The memory did not arrive as a photograph. It arrived as a re-entry. When the smell of diesel fuel hit his nose, or when a heavy hand accidentally brushed his shoulder in a crowded café, his body would instantly return to the shelter. His vision would tunnel, his chest would tighten, and the exact spot on his collarbone would throb with a sharp, familiar pain. He could not sit through the wave. The emotion would crest so fast he had to step away, grip the edge of a table, and wait for the air to return. What frightened him most was the certainty that the memory was not over; it was happening right now, and the threat was still present. His days became a series of quiet checks and deliberate silences. He would wake during the night, heart hammering against his ribs, and pad through the apartment to verify the locks, the window, the darkness. Even when his girlfriend, Mei, found him pacing at three in the morning, wrapping her arms around his back and insisting he was safe, the words landed on him like water on stone. He loved her, but even when others told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe it. The fear of harm had become a constant compass. A missed train, a delayed meeting, a text that went unanswered—each pause felt like a crack in the floor. He would assume something bad was happening, his mind already rehearsing worst-case scenarios. He had come to believe that you can never know who will harm you. Alongside the sleepless nights and the constant scanning, Thong had developed a quiet routine of physical and emotional restraint. He avoided eating, restricting his food to small portions of broth or skipping meals entirely. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger, fearing it would make him unpredictable or unworthy. At work, as a journalist covering municipal transit and public safety, these habits hardened into professional distance. When a male editor requested a follow-up interview in a private back office, Thong would politely decline, citing scheduling conflicts. He began taking the subway to avoid the bus, though the underground tunnels sometimes sparked the same frantic checks. When he did ride the bus to cover a city council meeting, he would sit near the doors, knees locked, eyes fixed on the passing poles, watching the other male passengers with a quiet, exhausting vigilance. The turning point came on a Tuesday in October. He had agreed to attend a press briefing downtown, but when a male source began walking beside him down the hallway, placing a hand on his shoulder, Thong felt his breath vanish. He stepped away, muttered an excuse, and left the building. Walking to the bus stop, he realized he could no longer ignore the architecture of his own days. He sat on a bench outside a community clinic, the weight of six months of isolation, skipped meals, and fractured sleep pressing down on him. He wanted to sleep through the night. He wanted to read his notes without his hands shaking. He was afraid of the next confrontation, but more than that, he hoped someone might help him untangle the belief that he was still standing in that bus shelter. He had finally dialed the number for trauma-informed therapy.
